stem: A and B were married, both Filipinos. A year after, B went to Hongkong for work. While B was in HK, A, knowing fully well that B was alive, while in full communication with B, filed a petition for presumptive death of B. 4 years after B left, A filed a petition for declaration of presumptive death which was granted by the court. 8 months after the decision, A married C. C is a high school batchmate of A and B. Status of the marriage between A and C?
choices: Valid, since A obtained a judicial declaration of presumptive death; but if both A and C acted in bad faith, the subsequent marriage is void (FC 44)
Voidable at the instance of B
Void ab initio in all cases because A did not actually believe B was dead, regardless of C's good faith
Valid in all cases, and B's reappearance has no effect
explanation: Atty. Uribe's answer: VALID as far as A is concerned, because A obtained a final judicial declaration of presumptive death ('sisihin mo si Judge'). The subsequent marriage remains valid until terminated by the recording of an affidavit of reappearance (Art. 42); termination presupposes a valid marriage. But if BOTH A and C acted in bad faith, the marriage is void ab initio under Art. 44. C was a high-school batchmate of both, so her knowledge that B was alive must be proved. Do not promise the client.
key_note: Debatable: Tolentino (PDF p. 172) submits that where the present spouse knew the absentee was alive, the subsequent marriage is void as bigamous because the Art. 41 element of a well-founded belief is wanting. Santos v. Santos (2014) holds that a fraudulently obtained declaration of presumptive death may be set aside by annulment of judgment (Rule 47), after which the marriage is bigamous. This item follows Atty. Uribe's answer.

stem: A and B are spouses. B went to Singapore on a four-year work contract and kept constant communication with A. In B's third year abroad, A obtained a judicial declaration of B's presumptive death, which became final. Months later A married C. B returned to the Philippines on January 1, 2024, but no sworn statement of reappearance has been recorded. C gave birth to a child on September 15, 2024. Assuming the A-C marriage is valid (it has not been shown that both A and C acted in bad faith), the child is:
choices: Legitimate, because the child was conceived before the termination of the subsequent marriage
Illegitimate, because B had already reappeared when the child was born
Illegitimate, because the subsequent marriage was automatically terminated upon B's return
Legitimate only if the child was born before B's return
None of the above
explanation: Under Art. 42 the subsequent marriage is terminated only by the RECORDING of the sworn statement of reappearance, not by mere physical reappearance. Under Art. 43(1), children of the subsequent marriage CONCEIVED prior to its termination are legitimate. What matters is conception before termination, not birth before reappearance. No affidavit has been recorded, so the A-C marriage subsists and the child is legitimate. (If both A and C were in bad faith, the marriage would be void under Art. 44 and the child illegitimate.)

stem: A bigamous marriage falling under Article 41 may be void even if there is a judicial declaration of presumptive death and all the essential and formal requisites are present.
choices: True
False
explanation: Art. 44: 'If both spouses of the subsequent marriage acted in bad faith, said marriage shall be void ab initio' even if a judicial declaration of presumptive death was obtained and all the essential and formal requisites are present. A subsequent marriage that otherwise falls under Art. 41 can therefore still be void. (Source: Midterm #17, Statement 2.)

stem: Lito, a commercial airline co-pilot, disappeared in 1998 when his flight vanished over the Pacific Ocean; no trace of the plane or its passengers and crew was ever found, and Lito was never heard of again. He left behind his wife Lita. In 2008, without any judicial proceeding, Lita married Jaime. In 2010, while touring China, Lita saw Lito alive. If Lito is alive, what is the status of Lita's marriage to Jaime?
choices: The marriage is valid because Lita's marriage to Lito was terminated upon Lito's disappearance for more than seven years.
The marriage is valid. After an absence of more than 10 years, Lito is already presumed dead for all purposes.
The marriage is void. Lito's mere absence, however lengthy, is insufficient to authorize Lita to contract a subsequent marriage.
The marriage is void. If Lito is indeed alive, his marriage to Lita was never dissolved and they can resume their marital relations at any time.
explanation: Void. Under Art. 41 a subsequent marriage during the subsistence of a prior marriage is valid only if, besides the required absence and a well-founded belief of death, the present spouse obtained a judicial declaration of presumptive death in a summary proceeding. Lita married Jaime in 2008 without such a declaration, so however long Lito's absence, it did not authorize her to remarry. If Lito is alive, the Lita-Jaime marriage is bigamous and void (Art. 35(4)).
key_note: (d) also says 'void', but its reasoning is not the ground of nullity: the Lita-Jaime marriage is void because Lita remarried without a judicial declaration of presumptive death (Art. 41), which (c) states. (d) speaks only of the Lito-Lita marriage subsisting, which is a consequence, not the reason. The source key is (c).

stem: True or False. Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The lack of certificate of legal capacity does not affect the validity of the marriage.
2. The subsequent bigamous marriage shall be automatically terminated by the reappearance of the absent spouse.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true per the answer key. The certificate of legal capacity required of a foreigner (Art. 21) relates to the issuance of the license. Its absence is at most an irregularity under Art. 4, and the marriage remains valid if a license was issued and the parties in fact had capacity (cf. Garcia v. Recio, 2001). No. 2 is false. Under Art. 42 the subsequent marriage is automatically terminated by the RECORDING of the affidavit of reappearance in the civil registry, not by mere reappearance (SSS v. Vda. de Bailon, 2006).

statements: 1. The subsequent marriage referred to in Article 41 shall be automatically terminated by the mere reappearance of the absent spouse, even if no affidavit of reappearance is recorded.

2. The sworn statement of the fact and circumstances of reappearance may be recorded in the civil registry at the instance of any interested person, with due notice to the spouses of the subsequent marriage.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 2 is true. It is Art. 42, par. 2: the sworn statement is recorded 'at the instance of any interested person, with due notice to the spouses of the subsequent marriage and without prejudice to the fact of reappearance being judicially determined in case such fact is disputed.' No. 1 is false. Termination is by the recording, and mere reappearance, even if known to the spouses, does not terminate the subsequent marriage (Tolentino, PDF pp. 172-173; SSS v. Vda. de Bailon, 2006). 'Any interested person' includes either party to the two marriages or a child of the first marriage.

statements: 1. Under the Family Code, a subsequent marriage contracted in compliance with Article 41 is voidable at the instance of the reappearing spouse.
2. The children of the subsequent marriage conceived prior to its termination shall be considered legitimate.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Under the Civil Code such a marriage was annullable, but under the FC it is not among the voidable marriages in Art. 45. It is VALID until terminated under Art. 42 (Tolentino, PDF p. 172). No. 2 is true. It is Art. 43(1): children of the subsequent marriage conceived prior to its termination shall be considered legitimate, and their custody and support in case of dispute shall be decided by the court in a proper proceeding.

stem: Children of the subsequent marriage conceived after the reappearance of the absentee spouse shall be illegitimate.
choices: True
False
explanation: Under Art. 42 the subsequent marriage is terminated only upon the RECORDING of the sworn statement of reappearance, not upon the reappearance itself. Under Art. 43(1), children of the subsequent marriage conceived prior to its termination are legitimate. A child conceived after the absentee physically reappears but before the affidavit is recorded is therefore legitimate, so the statement is not absolutely true. Note: this compiled samplex keyed 'True'; this is incorrect because the marriage subsists, and children conceived during it are legitimate, until the affidavit of reappearance is recorded (Arts. 42, 43(1)).
key_note: Note: this compiled samplex keyed 'True'; this is incorrect because the marriage subsists, and children conceived during it are legitimate, until the affidavit of reappearance is recorded (Arts. 42, 43(1)).

statements: 1. Upon termination of the subsequent marriage under Article 42, the absolute community or conjugal partnership shall be dissolved and liquidated, and the share in the net profits of the spouse who contracted the marriage in bad faith shall be forfeited in favor of the innocent spouse, or if there be none, the common children.
2. Donations by reason of marriage shall remain valid, except that if the donee contracted the marriage in bad faith, such donations made to said donee are revoked by operation of law.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Art. 43(2) forfeits the bad-faith spouse's share in the net profits 'in favor of the COMMON CHILDREN or if there be none, the children of the guilty spouse by a previous marriage or in default of children, the innocent spouse.' The statement reverses the order of beneficiaries. No. 2 is true: it is Art. 43(3) verbatim.

stem: A's wife B disappeared at sea in 2019 under circumstances of danger of death. In 2022, A, who honestly believed B dead after a diligent search, obtained a judicial declaration of B's presumptive death and married C. C, however, knew all along that B was alive in Davao. Before the wedding A donated a house to C by reason of the marriage, and he later designated C as irrevocable beneficiary of his life insurance. In 2025, B's sworn statement of reappearance was recorded. Which of the following is CORRECT?
choices: The A-C marriage is void ab initio because C acted in bad faith
The donation to C is revoked by operation of law, and A may revoke C's designation as beneficiary even though it was stipulated as irrevocable
The donation to C remains valid because the marriage was valid until its termination
C may still inherit from A by will, though not by intestacy
None of the above
explanation: Only C acted in bad faith, so Art. 44, which requires that BOTH spouses acted in bad faith, does not apply. The A-C marriage was valid and was terminated by the recording of the affidavit (Art. 42). Art. 43 then applies against C, the party in bad faith. Donations by reason of marriage to the bad-faith donee are revoked by operation of law (par. 3), and the innocent spouse may revoke the bad-faith spouse's designation as insurance beneficiary even if irrevocable (par. 4). C is also disqualified to inherit from A by testate AND intestate succession (par. 5), and C's share in the net profits is forfeited (par. 2).

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. If both spouses of the subsequent marriage acted in bad faith, said marriage shall be void ab initio and all testamentary dispositions made by one in favor of the other may be revoked by either spouse.
2. Non-disclosure of a previous conviction by final judgment of the other party shall constitute fraud resulting in a voidable marriage.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Art. 44 provides that if both spouses of the subsequent marriage acted in bad faith, the marriage is void ab initio and all donations by reason of marriage and testamentary dispositions made by one in favor of the other 'are REVOKED BY OPERATION OF LAW'. No act of revocation by either spouse is needed. No. 2 is false. Art. 46(1) makes fraud only the non-disclosure of a previous conviction by final judgment of the other party 'of a crime involving MORAL TURPITUDE'.

stem: A's wife B disappeared in 2015. In 2020, A obtained a judicial declaration of B's presumptive death and married C. At the time of the marriage, both A and C knew that B was alive and was living in Cebu. The marriage of A and C is:
choices: Valid until terminated by the recording of an affidavit of reappearance
Voidable at the instance of B
Valid, because a judicial declaration of presumptive death was obtained
Void ab initio, and all donations by reason of marriage and testamentary dispositions made by one in favor of the other are revoked by operation of law
None of the above
explanation: Art. 44: if both spouses of the subsequent marriage acted in bad faith, that is, both knew the absent spouse was alive, the marriage is void ab initio. All donations by reason of marriage and testamentary dispositions made by one in favor of the other are revoked by operation of law. The judicial declaration of presumptive death does not save the marriage. Tolentino (PDF p. 173) adds that in such a case the marriage may be attacked collaterally at any time, even after the death of a spouse.

statements: 1. The effects provided for by paragraphs (2), (3), (4) and (5) of Article 43 and by Article 44 shall also apply in the proper cases to marriages which are declared void ab initio or annulled by final judgment under Articles 40 and 45.
2. All creditors of the spouses as well as of the absolute community or the conjugal partnership shall be notified of the proceedings for liquidation.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: Both statements are true and track Art. 50, pars. 1 and 3, FC. Under Diño v. Diño (2011) and Valdes v. RTC (1996), the liquidation rules of Art. 50 apply to marriages void under Art. 40 and annulled under Art. 45. They do not apply to marriages void on other grounds such as Art. 36, whose property relations are governed by Art. 147 or 148. The final judgment must also provide for the liquidation, partition and distribution of the properties, the custody and support of the common children, and the delivery of their presumptive legitimes (Art. 50, par. 2).

stem: Miko and Dinah started to live together as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage in 1984. 10 years after, they separated. In 1996, they decided to live together again, and in 1998, they got married. On 17 Feb. 2001, Dinah filed a complaint for declaration of nullity of her marriage with Miko on the ground of psychological incapacity under Art. 36, FC The court rendered the following decision: 1. "Declaring the marriage null and void; 2. Dissolving the regime of absolute community of property; and 3. Declaring that a decree of absolute nullity of marriage shall only be issued after liquidation, partition and distribution of the parties' properties under Art. 147, FC. Dinah filed a motion for partial reconsideration questioning the portion of the decision on the issuance of a decree of nullity of marriage only after the liquidation, partition and distribution of properties under Art. 147, FC. If you are the judge, how will you decide petitioner's motion for partial reconsideration?
choices: Grant it, because Art. 50 and the requirement of prior liquidation apply only to marriages void under Art. 40 or annulled under Art. 45, not to marriages void under Art. 36.
Deny it, because under Art. 50 a decree of nullity may issue only after liquidation, partition and distribution of the properties.
Deny it, because the absolute community must first be liquidated before any decree may be issued.
Grant it, because no property regime exists in a void marriage, so there is nothing to liquidate.
explanation: Grant the motion. Diño v. Diño (2011): Art. 50 and Sec. 19(1) of A.M. No. 02-11-10-SC, which provide that the decree issues only after liquidation, partition and distribution, apply only to marriages declared void under Art. 40 or annulled under Art. 45. A marriage void under Art. 36 never produced an absolute community or conjugal partnership. The property relations are governed by co-ownership under Art. 147 (or 148), which may be liquidated under the Civil Code rules on co-ownership. The decree of nullity therefore issues upon finality of the judgment without awaiting liquidation (see also Valdes v. RTC, 1996).

stem: In the partition under Article 51 of the Family Code, the value of the presumptive legitimes of all common children shall be computed as of:
choices: The date of the celebration of the marriage
The date of the filing of the petition
The date of the final judgment of the trial court
The date of the death of either parent
None of the above
explanation: Art. 51, FC: 'In said partition, the value of the presumptive legitimes of all common children, computed as of the date of the final judgment of the trial court, shall be delivered in cash, property or sound securities, unless the parties, by mutual agreement judicially approved, had already provided for such matters.' The children, their guardian or the trustee of their property may ask for enforcement. The delivery does not prejudice the children's ultimate successional rights. The value received is considered an advance on their legitime.

The judgment of annulment or of absolute nullity of the marriage, the partition and distribution of the properties of the spouses, and the delivery of the children's presumptive legitimes shall be recorded in the appropriate civil registry and registries of property; otherwise, the same shall be void.
2. Either of the former spouses may marry again after compliance with the requirements of Article 52; otherwise, the subsequent marriage shall be null and void.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Art. 52 provides that if these are not recorded, 'the same shall NOT AFFECT THIRD PERSONS'. The judgment and partition are not void, only unenforceable against third persons. No. 2 is true. It is Art. 53, and the subsequent marriage contracted without compliance is the void marriage referred to in Art. 35(6). Children conceived or born of that subsequent marriage are nonetheless legitimate (Art. 54).

stem: A died, and A's surviving spouse later remarried without liquidating the property regime of the first marriage. After the surviving spouse also died, his heirs claimed that the subsequent marriage was void because there was no delivery of the presumptive legitimes of the children of the first marriage. The heirs are correct.
choices: True
False
explanation: Arts. 52-53 (recording of partition and delivery of presumptive legitimes as a condition for remarriage) apply only where the former marriage ended by annulment or judicial declaration of nullity. They do not apply where it was dissolved by death. When a surviving spouse remarries without first liquidating the community or conjugal property of the dissolved marriage, the sanction is that a mandatory regime of complete separation of property governs the subsequent marriage (Arts. 103 and 130, FC). The subsequent marriage remains valid.

stem: Children conceived and born outside a valid marriage are illegitimate.
choices: True
False
explanation: Not absolutely true. As a rule, children conceived and born outside a valid marriage are illegitimate (Art. 165), but Art. 54 provides exceptions. Children conceived or born before the judgment of absolute nullity under Art. 36 becomes final and executory are legitimate, and so are children conceived or born of a subsequent marriage void under Art. 53. Both are born of void marriages yet are legitimate.

stem: If a child was born after the judicial declaration of nullity of his parents' marriage, the child is illegitimate.
choices: True
False
explanation: Not necessarily. Under Art. 54, children CONCEIVED (or born) before the judgment of absolute nullity under Art. 36 becomes final and executory are legitimate. A child conceived during an Art. 36 marriage but born after the decree is legitimate. For other grounds of nullity, such as want of a license or incestuous or public-policy marriages, children conceived and born of the void marriage are illegitimate (Art. 165), except those of Art. 53 marriages.

stem: Children conceived or born before the promulgation of judgment of annulment or absolute nullity of the marriage under Article 36 shall be considered legitimate.
choices: True
False
explanation: Art. 54: 'Children conceived or born before the judgment of annulment or absolute nullity of the marriage under Article 36 has become final and executory shall be considered legitimate.' Every child conceived or born before promulgation is necessarily conceived or born before finality, so the statement is true as to all the children it covers. (The Midterm variant, 'conceived and born before the judgment ... has become final and executory', is likewise true.)

stem: Children born after the dissolution of the marriage of the parents may be legitimate.
choices: True
False
explanation: 'May be' makes this true. A child conceived during a valid marriage but born after its dissolution, for instance after the husband's death, is legitimate (Arts. 164, 168). Under Art. 54, children conceived before the judgment of annulment, or of nullity under Art. 36, becomes final are legitimate even if born afterwards. So are children of a subsequent marriage under Art. 53.
